item.title: “Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a…
item.description:
“Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a defilement of the mind; thinks: ‘Ill-will is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons ill-will, the defilement of the mind; anger … hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity; thinks: ‘Heedlessness is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons heedlessness, the defilement of the mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta

item.title: Elder Mahākāla: One who does not know thus, Yet still creates attachments — The fool goes on, Experiencing suffering again and again. Therefore, one who…
item.description:
Elder Mahākāla:

One who does not know thus,
Yet still creates attachments —
The fool goes on,
Experiencing suffering again and again.
Therefore, one who knows
Does not create attachments.
I will not lie down
With my head broken.

From: Theragāthā 2.16

item.title: "The monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and…
item.description:
"The monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He drenches, saturates, fills, and pervades his very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that no spot on his entire body is not pervaded by that rapture and pleasure born of seclusion."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta

item.title: The Blessed One replied to Upasīva: “Mindful, not longing for anything, You will cross the flood. Abandoning sensual desires, free from doubt, Day and night…
item.description:
The Blessed One replied to Upasīva:
“Mindful, not longing for anything,
You will cross the flood.
Abandoning sensual desires, free from doubt,
Day and night see clearly —
The destruction of craving is Nibbāna.”

“One who is completely dispassionate
Toward all sensual pleasures,
Depending on nothing, giving up all else —
Freed completely, that is the supreme liberation.
There, that one abides,
And does not go on.”

“Just as a flame blown by strong wind
Goes to its end and cannot be measured,
So too the sage, freed from name and body,
Goes to his end and cannot be measured.”

“For one who has reached the end,
There is no measure by which one could speak of him.
When all phenomena are uprooted,
All paths of speech are uprooted as well.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.7

item.title: Venerable Ajita: “By what is the world shrouded? Why does it not shine forth? What do you call its defilement? What is its great fear?”…
item.description:
Venerable Ajita:
“By what is the world shrouded?
Why does it not shine forth?
What do you call its defilement?
What is its great fear?”

The Blessed One:
“The world is shrouded by ignorance.
Through stinginess and heedlessness it does not shine forth.
I say longing is its defilement —
Suffering is its great fear.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.2

item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.33

item.title: “Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will…
item.description:
“Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful—all of them, having known as they actually are the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, with craving for sensual pleasures abandoned and the fever of sensual pleasures removed, have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta

item.title: “Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet…
item.description:
“Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet his mind is not liberated from the defilements without clinging. Why is that? It is because he has not developed. Not developed what? He has not developed the four foundations of mindfulness. He has not developed the four right efforts. He has not developed the four bases of spiritual power. He has not developed the five faculties. He has not developed the five powers. He has not developed the seven factors of enlightenment. He has not developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.101

item.title: “Monks, dwell contemplating foulness in the body. Establish well mindfulness of breathing, setting mindfulness before you, inwardly directed. Dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things.…
item.description:
“Monks, dwell contemplating foulness in the body. Establish well mindfulness of breathing, setting mindfulness before you, inwardly directed. Dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things. For one dwelling contemplating foulness in the body, the underlying tendency to lust for the beautiful is abandoned. For one who has well-established mindfulness of breathing, setting mindfulness before you, inwardly directed, there are no externally directed, harmful thoughts. For one dwelling contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.

Contemplating foulness in the body,
Mindful of in-breath and out-breath,
Calming all conditioned things,
Ever ardent, right in view —

That monk who sees rightly,
From that, being thus liberated,
Perfects direct knowledge,
Is at peace, truly stilled —
That sage has certainly crossed beyond all yokes.”

From: Itivuttaka 85

item.title: “And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. This, monks, is called right effort.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.8
